title: Open with a claim, not a definition
body:
Take the question "Examine the impact of urbanization on Indian cities". Most answers start by explaining what urbanization means. The examiner already knows.

In the topper copies we studied, the strongest openings take a position on the question in the first sentence.

title: Two or three numbers, not twenty
body:
A claim with nothing behind it reads weak. A claim with one well-chosen number reads strong.

Pick three or four data points you can reuse across many questions, instead of memorising twenty statistics per subject.

title: The 7-minute answer
body:
You get about 7 minutes per Mains answer.

First minute: read the question twice, underline the demand, pick an angle.
Next five: write without stopping.
Last minute: underline key terms, add a diagram if it helps, close with a sentence.

People who run out of time usually started writing before they knew what to say.

title: Short paragraphs get read
body:
Keep paragraphs to three to five sentences, sometimes two. Long paragraphs get skimmed. Short ones make the examiner read every line.

Underline the key term in a sentence, just the word, not the whole line.

title: Write one answer a day, then review it
body:
Writing four answers a day does not help if you never compare them with a good one.

For two weeks, write one answer a day. Spend 20 minutes comparing it with how a topper answered a similar question, and rewrite your opening sentence.

title: A diagram only when it says something faster
body:
In the copies we studied, toppers drew a diagram in about one answer out of four or five. A clean flowchart of cause, mechanism and effect can carry a paragraph. A weak diagram only costs time.

If a diagram does not say something faster than words, skip it.

title: Read the question twice
body:
Most lost marks in Mains come from answering a different question from the one asked. Underline the directive word (examine, discuss, critically analyse) and the topic, and answer exactly that.

A 10 second pause at the start saves a rewritten answer at the end.

title: Prelims: the skip decision
body:
GS Paper I has 100 questions for 200 marks. A right answer earns 2, a wrong one loses 0.66, a skip is 0. Two hours for 100 questions is about 72 seconds each.

Practise deciding when to skip, under the real marking.

title: Prelims: eliminate before you guess
body:
If you can remove two options with confidence, a guess among the other two has better odds than a blind one. If you cannot remove any, skipping is often the right call.

Train the elimination habit on past papers, not on the day.

title: Statements questions: find the extreme word
body:
In a statement question, words like always, only, all and never make a statement easy to test. One counter-example is enough to mark it wrong.

Check the extreme statements first. They often settle the answer.

title: Revise by recall, not by rereading
body:
Closing the notes and writing down what you remember beats a third reading. Do it at the end of each study block: five minutes, a blank page, then check what you missed.

The gaps you find are your next revision list.

title: Make one-page notes per topic
body:
Long notes are rarely revised. After finishing a topic, compress it to one page: definitions, a few numbers, two examples, one diagram.

A subject you can revise in a day is a subject you will revise five times.

title: Read the newspaper with a pen
body:
Do not read everything. Pick three stories a day, and for each write one line on what happened and one line on why it matters for governance, economy or international relations.

That habit is worth more than two hours of scrolling.

title: Link every current affairs story to the syllabus
body:
Before you save a news item, name the syllabus topic it belongs to. If you cannot, it probably does not belong in your notes.

This keeps your current affairs file short and useful.

title: The interview starts from your DAF
body:
In the 14 transcripts of CSE 2025 interviews we read, about a third of the questions came straight from the DAF.

Read every line of your form as if a stranger will question you on it, and mark each item you cannot explain in two sentences.

title: Prepare your home district
body:
Boards often ask about the candidate's home state and district: economy, issues, schemes, history, people.

Write a one-page note on yours before any mock interview.

title: Three to five mocks, spaced out
body:
More mock interviews do not always help. Each one gives you new things to fix, but only if you leave time to fix them.

Space three to five mocks across the weeks before your date, with a few days between each.

title: Before you pick an optional
body:
Read two years of its question papers. If you can picture yourself answering them, that is a good sign.

A few marks of difference in medians matters far less than your interest and how much syllabus you can finish twice before Mains.

title: Finish the optional syllabus twice
body:
One pass teaches you the subject. The second pass, with answer writing, is where the marks come from.

Work backwards from your Mains date and fix when pass two starts.

title: Essay: spend the first ten minutes on structure
body:
Pick the topic you can say the most about, not the one that sounds the grandest. Write a two-line thesis and three or four paragraph headings before you write a sentence.

An essay with a clear spine scores better than a long one that wanders.

title: Ethics: use a real case
body:
In GS4 case studies, name the stakeholders, the values in conflict, the options and your choice with a reason. Then add what you would do to prevent it next time.

Examiners reward a clear decision with a reason more than a long list.

title: Test series: analyse more than you attempt
body:
A test you attempt and never analyse teaches little. After each one, list the questions you got wrong or guessed, and why.

A smaller series you analyse properly beats a large one you leave half done.

title: Ask three things before paying for any course
body:
What is the refund term? How fast do answers come back? Can I see a sample evaluated copy?

If an institute will not answer in writing, that tells you something.

title: Know the marks target
body:
The Mains cut-off for the General category was 748 in CSE 2022, 741 in 2023 and 729 in 2024. Crossing it gets you an interview. The rank comes from written plus interview.

Work out your target per paper, then check your mocks against it.

title: Do not copy a topper's timetable
body:
A timetable works for the person who built it around their own job, health and habits. Copy the principle (fixed hours, weekly revision, regular tests), not the hours.

Try one for a week, then adjust.

title: Plan the week on Sunday
body:
Spend 20 minutes each Sunday listing the topics, tests and revision blocks for the week, and what you will drop if you fall behind.

A plan with a drop list survives a bad day.

title: Sleep is part of the syllabus
body:
Recall and writing speed both fall when you are short of sleep. Treat a fixed sleep time as part of your plan, not a reward for finishing it.

One extra hour of sleep can be worth more than one extra hour of reading.

title: Use the free topper data
body:
Marks of past toppers, paper by paper, tell you where marks are won. The biggest gaps between top rankers and the rest are often in GS2 and the essay.

Check the paper-by-paper numbers before you decide where to spend your next month.

title: When you feel behind
body:
Almost every aspirant feels behind at some point. Compare your plan with your own last month, not with someone else's highlight reel.

Pick the one topic you will finish this week and finish it.
